content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a structured pruning strategy for Winograd convolution which can take on a row or column sparse format. Compared with the irregular pruning of Winograd filters, the proposed pruning has lower latency due to better data indexing. Compared to Winograd filter pruning, this method can achieve higher latency for the same latency speedup since it supports a lower pruning granularity than that of removing entire filters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The performance gains for the proposed method over the two baselines, i.e., irregular Wingorad pruning and filter pruning, are good.
- The paper has lots of visualizations to better convey the pruning and Winograd convolution methodology. However, the figures were a bit too detailed which made them complex to read, perhaps they can be simplified and some of the less important details can be removed.

Weaknesses:
- While the proposed method performs well in terms of accuracy and latency, it is not necessarily very novel. The proposed pruning is very similar to the filter pruning with only a minor modification to the granularity. The pruning technique itself, i.e., using lasso regularization, is also well-studied in the prior art.
- Perhaps it will be interesting to see how the proposed pruning compares with SOTA pruning of standard convolution in the benchmarked models (ResNet-18 and VGG-16). Many recent works show impressive pruning ratios for these benchmarks with negligible accuracy drop so is it possible that the higher pruning ratio achieved in standard convolution can surpass the latency benefits of pruned Winograd convolution?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper (as the title suggests) proposes a structured pruning in the winograd domain to speed-up the inference of convolutional layers of neural networks with minimal error drop.

The paper provides a good background overview of current approaches for pruning of winograd based convolutional layers. This overview is though, a bit too detailed and takes a large amount of page real estate.

The authors then propose their structured pruning - which is nothing new - pruning sub-vectors of the "transformed matrices" so that the vector units of the underlying hardware can be utilized (thread warps in the GPU case).

The authors then evaluate their approach on a well studied (and relatively easy) dataset - ImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The biggest strength of the paper is the detailed overview of the Winograd pruning approaches. However, such detailed overview is not a good fit for a paper of this kind (where only a tiny incremental alleged novelty is proposed).

What authors do explain, but not clearly and explicitly mention, is that the second stage of the winograd transform is just a set of matrix-matrix multiplications. And depending on how the matrices are arranged (and whether the computaiton is batched) different matrix-multiplication algorithms can be used.

This is the biggest weakness of the paper. The authors don't consider well known and studied sparse matrix-matrix multiplications which can be directly used in the second stage of the winograd convolution. That being said - studying "block-sparse" matrix multiplication is the equivalent problem to what the authors propose (just applied to the second stage of the winograd algorithm).

This idea is not new. And while I don't remember seing it directly applied to the second stage of the winograd algorithm,  the novelty of doing so doesn't raise to the level of this venue.

The evaluation of the approach on a single data set, and single network is another huge weakness of the author's work (as is the case in a lot of CNN pruning papers). The ImageNet is well understood and relatively easy dataset, and VGG used has great capacity - it is not a surprise that this pruning approach works well (nor would be surprise if other pruning approaches worked well).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is very clear. The quality of the work doesn't raise to the level of this venue.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the authors present their proposed approach clearly in a well structured paper - the level of novelty of the proposed approach is way below for what would be expected at Neurips. That, combined with a choice to only evaluate the approach on a single well studied and easy dataset, and one network makes the work very weak.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a structured pruning method specialized for Winograd convolution. The main insight is that element-wise Winograd pruning is performing but suffers from limited hardware support and filter-wise Winograd pruning is unit too aggressive to preserve accuracy. This paper utilizes group lasso to find a trade-off between element-wise pruning and filter-wise pruning, constraining the pruned weights to be rows and columns that can be hardware efficient and yield speed up.  Experiments on ResNets & VGG on CIFAR and ImageNet show that the WSP-C suffers from less accuracy drop than common structured pruning methods, like SFP and FPGM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

(1) The authors first motivate by the drawbacks of Winograd weight pruning and filter pruning, based on which they naturally introduce group-wise Winograd pruning. The storyline of the paper is natural and smooth. 

(2) Using group LASSO is a straightforward choice to induce group-level sparsity and the speedup over the filter-level pruning is promising.

## Weakness

(1) The technical novelty of this paper is limited. Group LASSO is already a mutual technique whose effectiveness has been widely demonstrated on normal convolutional neural networks. Are there any daunting difficulties of applying group LASSO to Winograd convolution?  

(2) The experimental evaluation of WSP is insufficient. This paper compares WSP (a group-level pruning method) with several filter-level pruning approaches (mainly proposed in 2017-2019). This is not an apple-to-apple comparison. I highly recommend authors compare with state-of-the-art group-level pruning methods (for instance "Group Sparsity: The Hinge Between Filter Pruning and Decomposition for
Network Compression", etc.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-motivated and the proposed method is sound.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is well-motivated and supported by good results. My main concern is the limited technical novelty overall. And the unfair comparison reported in Table 1 is unable to demonstrate the true strength of WSP.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper focuses on the problem of achieving high performance CNN inference on GPUs without compromising on accuracy. Two techniques that have been previously used for this application are Winograd convolution (WC, no accuracy loss) and Pruning (accuracy loss as pruning ratio increases), while both techniques help improve performance, optimally combining them isn’t straightforward. Existing implementations of this combination aren’t optimal for GPU hardware for e.g., Winograd Weight Pruning (WWP): Irregular data-access resulting in low perf and Filter Pruning (FP) – Low accuracy for high-perf.  

This paper proposes another technique that combines WC with Pruning: Winograd Structured Pruning (WSP). WSP applies structured pruning in the Winograd domain which allows regular mem access patterns without loss of accuracy enabling high performance. It also defines a threshold for the pruning unit size to ensure it doesn’t become too large thereby limiting its accuracy losses. 

The authors demonstrate how WSP achieves better performance (1.8x and 2.9x) with low accuracy loss (<1%) than WWP and FP techniques for VGG-16 CNN trained on ImageNet dataset. Similar performance improvement is demonstrated for ResNet-18 CNN trained on ImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The authors provide a clear description of Winograd transform and Pruning methods used to speed up CNN inference while also explaining the intricacies of implementing it on a GPU HW. They have provided a well-rounded section describing prior art in this domain. They also employ detailed figures throughout the paper which are very helpful in clearly communicating the ideas presented in this paper. The proposed WSP technique enables more fine-grained structured pruning than FP while maintaining the accuracy benefits of pruning in the Winograd domain. 

Figure 4 highlights that at very high pruning ratios the inference time for WWP approach can be lower than dense CNN implementation. However, the results in Figure 8 show that WWP performance always worse than dense CNN. Why aren’t these two figures consistent on this aspect? Similarly, it is surprising that FP method which prunes much larger number of weights for the most time consuming EWMM step is always worse on performance compared to WSP in Figure 8. Further, as shown in Figure 6 WWP approach can achieve high accuracy inference even at very high pruning ratios. Shouldn’t the high pruning ratios allow the irregular memory access penalty for WWP to be lower? Also, just for completeness, can the authors add WSP-R also to Figure 8 since it is deployed on a few of the layers for the final speedup improvement result (1.8x and 2.9x). Lastly, adding FP filter visualizations to Figure 10 might help understand how WSP achieves much better performance than FP. 

Table 1 shows a comparison of the proposed techniques against a few prior art approaches. It would be helpful if the authors could include a description of some of the unique features of these references in Section 3. Could the authors also elaborate the comment, “Since WSP can prune only 3 convolutional layers, WSP-C performs filter pruning (groupLASSO) on the FC layer”? Are different approaches applying filter pruning to selective layers only? How are the authors selecting the appropriate layers for applying filter pruning? 

In Section 4.2, authors describe high sensitivity to pruning, can they please elaborate more on this? Does this mean that features that are important for CNN inference are removed? Authors also mention a developing a customized code for WSP-C to enable a dense-BGEMM. Does the FP approach have a similar code available to help exploit the performance benefit of structured pruning? Another key aspect is that the performance benefits gained due to this custom code are specific to GPU libraries and won’t extend to other parallel processors (for e.g., ARM/Intel). The authors should quantify how much performance benefit they achieve through the custom code. 

Could the authors shed some light on why they selected the specific CNN models (VGG-16 and ResNet-18) for their experiments? It makes sense that training deeper/more complex models with pruning while ensuring low accuracy drop is challenging, but it might also enable more speedup for the larger models which have much larger layers which might exhibit even higher sparsity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors have done a great job of explaining the complex topics discussed in the paper, however a few sections of the paper are difficult to follow. For instance, the authors mention WSP-C/R in Section 1 before going through the description of WSP which is a bit confusing, consider removing the classification of WSP-C/R in Section 1. In Section 2.2, using #1 and #a to denote both the element marker as well as the matrix marker makes the section very hard to read, please consider using some other unique label e.g., Greek letters to distinguish these two. 

Minor issues, Section 2.2 please add reference for the claim that ARM measurements suggest EWMM is the most time-consuming step of WC on parallel processors. Adding the full form for CSR and NPU (Section 4.1) will help improve the readability. There seems to be some inconsistency towards the end of Section 4.1 in the following sentences: 1) “However, the effect of FP is not appreciable, because it is limited to pruning ratio. “, 2) “Therefore, although FP is hardware-friendly structured, and even re-training is applied, FP has a significant accuracy drop in the high pruning ratio. Therefore, structured pruning with high pruning ratio needs to be applied to WC. “, please consider rewriting these sentences. 

Questions related to the quality of a few results are mentioned in the Strengths/Weaknesses section.
content.summary_of_the_review: In conclusion, the authors present an interesting combination of pruning and Winograd convolution that enables high accuracy/performance CNN inference on parallel processors. While the authors’ presentation (figures/discussion) is good and the results indicate significant benefit from the proposed technique on parallel processors, some aspects of the discussion of results are incomplete. Adding the required discussion will help consolidate the presented results and refine the paper.

content.title: Winograd Structured Pruning for Fast Winograd Convolution
content.TL;DR: We propose a novel Winograd structured pruning method, which prunes the weights in the Winograd-domain in a structured form with optimized pruning unit size for fast Winograd convolution on parallel processors.
content.abstract:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are computationally intensive, which limits deployment into mobile devices.  
To minimize operation counts in CNNs, pruning optimization techniques and Winograd’s minimal filtering algorithm are widely used; however, the benefit of pruning disappears when both optimizations are simply applied together in CNN. 
To take full advantage of both approaches, two previous pruning methods were proposed: one is to apply pruning after kernel transformation, and the other is applying filter pruning on Winograd convolution. 
Unfortunately, the first method is hardware-unfriendly and the second approach suffers from a significant loss of accuracy.
Thus, we propose structured pruning method specialized for Winograd convolution, that maximizes the hardware utilization by considering the conversion algorithm of parallel processors. 
We analyze the conversion algorithm of Winograd convolution on parallel processing units; then, we prune the weights in the Winograd-domain in a structured form with optimized pruning unit size, which maximizes the parallelism of the hardware while minimizing the loss of accuracy. 
For VGG-16 on the ImageNet dataset, the inference time of our method is $1.84$ and $2.89$ times better than previous two pruning methods with less than $1\%$ accuracy loss.
